production.title: Claude Fable 5.2 vs Opus 5.5: 10 Real Builds (Opus Still Wins!!)

narration:
On November 9, 2026, Anthropic released a model with a 1-million-token memory,
a maximum answer length of 128,000 tokens,
and an API price of $8 for every million
input tokens and $40 for every million output tokens.
That model is Fable 5.2, and it isn't designed mainly for quick questions.
It's designed for the job you give an AI,
then leave running while it reads, plans, writes,
tests and comes back with something finished.
The obvious comparison is Opus 5.5,
the model Anthropic still recommends for most everyday work.
So which one should you use, and what is Fable actually better at?
By the end of this video, you'll know what changed,
why Fable and the restricted Mythos model are connected,
how to choose between Fable and Opus,
and how to give Fable a long technical job
without just throwing a vague prompt at it.
The story starts with a model most people weren't allowed to use.
Alongside Fable 5.2, Anthropic announced Mythos 5.2.
The company describes them as having the same underlying model.
The difference is access and safeguards.
Fable is the generally available version, with stronger protections around cybersecurity and biology.
Mythos is reserved for organisations that pass Anthropic's verification programmes.
So this wasn't simply a new name for the normal chatbot.
It was a model built for work that can be useful,
but can also become risky if the instructions are wrong.
In its November 9 announcement,
Anthropic said prerelease testing used Fable 5.2 on difficult software migrations,
robotics tasks and the design of 3 working electronic devices.
It also said the model made progress on 2 open problems in black-hole physics.
That sounds extraordinary, but keep the wording honest.
These are demonstrations reported by the company,
not independent proof that the model has solved
physics or can replace a research team.
The important part for you is not the black-hole headline.
It's the type of work being tested.
Long codebases.
Technical research.
Engineering constraints.
Tasks where the answer is only useful if
the model keeps track of the whole problem.
That is the gap Fable is meant to fill.
But to understand why,
you need to look at what happens inside a long job.
A normal chat often works like this.
You ask a question, get an answer and decide what to ask next.
A long-running model works more like a contractor.
You give it a brief, it keeps the brief in view,
works through several stages and produces a document,
a code change or another finished result at the end.
Fable 5.2 has a 1-million-token context window.
Tokens are small pieces of text, not exactly words,
so this is not the same as memorising a million ordinary words.
But it is enough room for a large codebase, a long technical report,
a set of research papers or a detailed
project history to stay available during one task.
The model can also produce up to 128,000 tokens in one response.
That matters when the result is not a paragraph, but a migration plan,
a large code change, a spreadsheet or a presentation.
And its thinking is adaptive.
The reasoning is always available,
while an effort setting controls how much work the model spends before answering.
A simple request does not need the same depth as a difficult engineering problem.
Here's the practical tip:
don't use a long-context model by pasting in everything you own.
Give it the files that define the job,
explain what a successful result looks like,
and tell it how to check its work.
For example, instead of saying, “Improve this project,” say, “Read the repository,
map the current architecture, identify the files that need changing, make the migration,
run the existing tests,
and report every test that still fails.” That turns the
model from a text generator into a process with checkpoints.
The long memory helps, but the instructions still determine whether the work is useful.
Now we can compare the 2 models properly.
Anthropic's own evaluations put Fable 5.2 ahead of Opus 5.5 on several tested tasks,
including FrontierSWE v2 for software work, AutomationBench for computer use, Terminal-Bench-Science, BenchCAD and Chartography.
Those names cover different abilities: changing real software, operating tools,
solving technical problems through a terminal, working with computer-aided design and producing accurate charts.
But “ahead on several evaluations” is not the same
as “wins every task.” Some comparisons were close,
and results changed with the effort setting.
Anthropic's own guidance is more measured than the online arguments.
Start with Opus 5.5 for normal coding and knowledge work.
Move to Fable 5.2 when Opus at higher effort still doesn't meet the requirement.
Fable also has 2 practical advantages, according to Anthropic.
It can generate answers up to 30% faster than Fable 5.1,
and its input and output pricing is 20% lower than the previous version.
The listed API price is $8 per million
input tokens and $40 per million output tokens,
compared with $10 and $50 for Fable 5.1.
Batch requests get a 50% discount.
The company also reports about 55% fewer unnecessary safeguard blocks than Fable 5.1.
That does not mean every request is allowed.
High-risk cybersecurity and biology work can still be blocked or sent to another model.
So the verdict here is simple: Opus is the sensible default.
Fable is the expensive, heavier tool you bring in when the job is long,
technical or costly to get wrong.
What does that mean in practice?
Start with a software migration.
Give Fable the repository, the current version,
the target version and the tests that must continue passing.
Ask it to inspect first, write a migration plan,
make the changes in stages and run the tests after each important step.
The useful part is not that it writes code quickly.
The useful part is that it can keep the old system,
the new requirements and the test results in the same working context.
You still review the changes,
but you spend less time copying the same background into 5 separate conversations.
The next use is deep research.
Give it a focused question,
the source material and the format you need at the end.
Ask it to separate facts from assumptions,
show where each important claim came from and mark anything it could not verify.
That last instruction matters.
A large context window gives the model more material to work with.
It does not automatically make every source reliable.
For engineering work, describe the constraints before asking for a design.
Include dimensions, materials, power limits,
safety requirements and the tests the design has to pass.
Anthropic says Fable was used to design 3 working electronic devices during testing.
That is a company-reported result,
not a reason to skip a qualified engineer or physical testing.
Fable can also produce finished artefacts: a document, spreadsheet or presentation.
The better workflow is to ask for an outline first, then the completed version,
then a quality check against the original brief.
If you need a financial spreadsheet, for example,
tell it which totals must reconcile and which
cells should contain formulas instead of typed numbers.
And for robotics or other physical systems, use it to connect the pieces:
sensor data, control logic, simulation and test results.
The model can help organise a workflow,
but a robot still has to be tested in the real world.
A correct-looking plan is not the same as a safe machine.
Across all of these examples, the same pattern keeps coming back.
Give Fable a large but relevant body of information, define the finished result,
ask for intermediate checks and make it show its evidence.
If you want to try Fable 5.2,
developers can call it through the model ID
`claude-fable-5-2` in the API and supported cloud platforms.
Access through an ordinary application depends on the plan and service you are using.
Set the effort level based on the job.
Use a lighter setting for a short transformation.
Use more effort when the model has to compare alternatives,
reason through constraints or repair its own work.
Then use a prompt with 4 parts: the goal, the material it can use,
the rules it must follow and the check it must perform before finishing.
For example: “Read these files.
Create a migration plan.
Apply the changes only after explaining the affected components.
Run the test suite.
Do not claim success unless the tests pass,
and list every failure with the file and line involved.” That
is much safer than asking for a miracle in one sentence.
Watch the cost, too.
A million input tokens and a million output
tokens would cost $48 at the listed rates,
although real jobs usually use different amounts.
Long context is useful, but unnecessary files and repeated output still increase the bill.
And don't confuse a completed response with a verified result.
Review code.
Check calculations.
Open the generated presentation.
Test the device.
Read the sources.
Fable can shorten the path to a finished draft,
but the responsibility for accepting the result is still yours.
So, Fable 5.2 is not simply Opus with a louder launch video.
It is a model aimed at long technical jobs, with a 1-million-token context,
adaptive effort, a 128,000-token output limit and lower listed pricing than Fable 5.1.
Use Opus 5.5 for ordinary work.
Reach for Fable when the task has many connected parts,
needs sustained reasoning and ends in something you can inspect and use.
The free guide to this video and the link to our community
for updates and more stories like this are in the description.
Follow the channel,
because the next useful comparison is not which model wins a benchmark,
but which one actually saves you time on the work you do.
The question is, what would you give Fable first: a large codebase,
a research project or a finished document you normally build by hand?

research.summary: Claude Fable 5.2 launched on November 9, 2026, alongside the restricted Claude Mythos 5.2. Anthropic describes them as the same underlying model: Fable is the generally available version with strong safeguards for cybersecurity and biology, while Mythos is reserved for organizations approved through Anthropic’s verification programs. The release is aimed at difficult, long-running technical work rather than ordinary chat. It supports a 1-million-token context window, up to 128,000 output tokens, and always-on adaptive thinking whose depth can be controlled with an effort setting. Fable 5.2 costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens—20% less than Fable 5.1—and Anthropic says it produces outputs up to 30% faster. Anthropic reports that its safeguards generated about 55% fewer unnecessary blocks than Fable 5.1, although high-risk cyber and biology requests can still be blocked or routed to another model. The model can be used for long-running coding agents, deep research, large migrations, engineering design, robotics workflows, and producing finished documents, spreadsheets, or presentations. Anthropic’s own guidance is more measured than the video’s headline: use Opus 5.5 as the normal daily model, then move to Fable 5.2 when Opus at higher effort does not meet the requirements. Benchmark results show Fable 5.2 ahead of Opus 5.5 on many evaluated tasks, but not literally every task, so “Opus still loses at everything” would be an unsupported conclusion.

claims.source_title: Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2

claims.claim: The intended user workflow is to employ Fable 5.2 for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks such as multistep research, large codebases, and work that must end in a finished document, spreadsheet, or presentation.

claims.claim: Developers can call Fable 5.2 with the model ID claude-fable-5-2 through the Claude API and supported cloud platforms; users can control reasoning depth with the effort parameter and use the model for long-running agentic workflows.

metadata.description:
Free guide to this video (steps and every source): https://studio.golidee.com/guides/golide-long-2026-11-10.pdf

Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 is built for long, technical jobs that require sustained reasoning, large files, code changes, research, testing, and finished deliverables. This video explains its 1-million-token context window, 128,000-token output limit, adaptive effort, pricing, and connection to the restricted Mythos 5.2 model.

We compare Fable 5.2 with Opus 5.5 and explain when each model makes sense. You’ll also learn how to prompt Fable for software migrations, deep research, engineering work, spreadsheets, presentations, and other tasks where verification matters.

The video covers practical workflows, cost considerations, safety limits, benchmark claims, and a reusable prompt structure for giving Fable a complex job without relying on a vague instruction.
